title: Machine Design
tagline: Static failure theories, fatigue, shafts, bearings, gears, fasteners and welded joints, springs, clutches, brakes, belts and chains
summary: Machine design sizes the components that make machines work so that they neither break nor wear out too soon. Building on mechanics of materials, the course covers failure theories for static loading, fatigue under fluctuating loads, and the design and selection of shafts, rolling and journal bearings, gears, threaded fasteners and welded joints, springs, and clutches, brakes, belts and chains.
overview: Machine design turns the stresses and deflections of [[mechanics-of-materials]] into the sizes, materials and tolerances of real machine elements: shafts, bearings, gears, bolts and welds, springs, clutches, brakes, belts and chains. Each element is designed to do its job for its intended life without yielding, breaking, wearing out or deflecting too much, and with a factor of safety that reflects how well the loads, the material and the consequences of failure are known.

The course begins with the two ideas on which everything else rests. Static failure theories — maximum shear stress (Tresca), distortion energy (von Mises) and the Coulomb–Mohr family for brittle materials — decide whether a part survives its largest load. Fatigue decides whether it survives its life: most machine parts that fail in service fail by cracks that grow under loads far below the yield strength, and the stress-life method, with its endurance limit, modifying factors, notch sensitivity and mean-stress criteria, is the designer's main tool against it.

The remaining chapters apply these ideas element by element. Shafts are sized for combined fatigue loading, deflection and critical speed; rolling bearings are selected from their rated life and journal bearings analysed by hydrodynamic lubrication; gear teeth are rated for root bending and surface contact; bolted joints are designed through preload and joint stiffness, and welds through their throat stresses; springs are designed for rate, stress, buckling, fatigue and surge; and friction elements are sized for torque and, usually more critically, for the heat they must dissipate.

Much of machine design rests on empirical data and design rules — surface factors, form factors, load ratings, allowable stresses — that come from tests and are codified in standards such as ISO 281, ISO 6336, ANSI/AGMA 2001, ISO 898-1, VDI 2230 and EN 13906. The course derives the mechanics behind them, says where each rule comes from and how far it can be trusted, and works every calculation with real numbers. It teaches the principles; real machines, and especially safety-critical ones such as lifting equipment, pressure equipment and vehicles, are designed to the current codes and checked by qualified engineers.
outcomes: Calculate factors of safety for ductile and brittle parts under static load with the Tresca, von Mises and Coulomb–Mohr criteria, including stress concentration where it matters.

Estimate the endurance limit of a real part from the Marin factors and the notch sensitivity, and calculate fatigue factors of safety and lives with the Goodman, Gerber and ASME-elliptic criteria and Miner's rule.
Size a shaft for combined fluctuating bending and torsion, and check its deflections, slopes and first critical speed, and its keys.
Select a rolling bearing from its rated life, equivalent load and required reliability, and analyse the friction and load capacity of a hydrodynamic journal bearing.
Calculate the forces on spur and helical gear teeth and their bending and contact stresses, and explain the structure of AGMA and ISO gear rating.
Design a bolted joint by choosing the preload and calculating the joint stiffness, bolt load, separation margin and fatigue factor of safety, and size fillet welds under direct and eccentric loads.
Design a helical compression spring for rate, static stress, buckling, fatigue and surge.
Size disc clutches and brakes for torque and heat, and belt and chain drives for tension, power and speed variation.

chapters.title: Failure under static loading
chapters.summary: Failure theories for ductile and brittle materials — maximum shear stress, distortion energy and Mohr–Coulomb — and stress concentration.

chapters.title: Fatigue failure
chapters.summary: S–N curves, endurance limits and modifying factors, fluctuating stresses with the Goodman and Gerber criteria, and cumulative damage.

chapters.title: Shafts and shaft components
chapters.summary: Shaft layout, stresses and deflections under combined loads, critical speeds, keys and couplings.

chapters.title: Rolling and journal bearings
chapters.summary: Rolling-bearing life, load ratings and selection, and the hydrodynamic lubrication of journal bearings.

chapters.title: Gear design
chapters.summary: Gear geometry and force analysis of meshes, bending and contact stresses in gear teeth, and gear rating.

chapters.title: Fasteners and welded joints
chapters.summary: Threaded fasteners, bolt preload and joint stiffness, and bolted, welded and bonded joints under static and fatigue loads.

chapters.title: Mechanical springs
chapters.summary: Helical compression, extension and torsion springs: stresses, deflection, buckling, fatigue and surge.

chapters.title: Clutches, brakes, belts and chains
chapters.summary: Friction clutches and brakes with their energy dissipation and temperature rise, and power transmission by belts and chains.

history.title: Coulomb's laws of friction
history.detail: Charles-Augustin Coulomb's *Théorie des machines simples*, which won the Paris Academy's prize of 1781, was published in 1785; its experimental laws of dry friction underlie the design of clutches, brakes and belt drives.

history.title: First fatigue tests
history.detail: Wilhelm Albert, a mining official at Clausthal, published tests of iron hoisting chains loaded repeatedly — the first recorded fatigue experiments.

history.title: Wöhler's axle tests
history.detail: August Wöhler completed the series of rotating-bending tests of railway axles and specimens that he had published since 1858, establishing the S–N curve, the endurance limit and the importance of the stress range.

history.title: Reynolds's theory of lubrication
history.detail: Following Beauchamp Tower's experiments of 1883–84 on oil pressure in a railway journal bearing, Osborne Reynolds published the hydrodynamic theory of lubrication on which journal-bearing design is based.

history.title: The Lewis equation for gear teeth
history.detail: Wilfred Lewis presented to the Engineers' Club of Philadelphia his analysis of the gear tooth as a cantilever of uniform strength, the starting point of all later gear bending-strength rating.

history.title: Distortion-energy yield criterion
history.detail: Richard von Mises proposed the yield criterion that, with the energy interpretations of Huber (1904) and Hencky (1924), became the standard static failure theory for ductile machine parts.

history.title: Miner's rule
history.detail: M. A. Miner published the linear cumulative-damage rule for fatigue under variable-amplitude loading, generalising a rule used by Arvid Palmgren for ball bearings in 1924.

history.title: Lundberg–Palmgren bearing life theory
history.detail: Gustaf Lundberg and Arvid Palmgren published their statistical theory of the dynamic load capacity of rolling bearings, the basis of the L10 life and of ISO 281.

references.title: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design
references.authors: R. G. Budynas and J. K. Nisbett
references.note: 11th edition (McGraw-Hill). The standard course text; the source of the fatigue factors, shaft, spring, bolted-joint and gear data used in this course.

references.title: Fundamentals of Machine Component Design
references.authors: R. C. Juvinall and K. M. Marshek
references.note: 7th edition (Wiley). Clear physical explanations of failure, fatigue and the design of machine elements, with many worked problems.

references.title: Machine Design: An Integrated Approach
references.note: 6th edition (Pearson). Strong on fatigue, shafts, gears and springs, with a design-case approach.

references.title: Mechanical Design of Machine Elements and Machines
references.authors: J. A. Collins, H. R. Busby and G. H. Staab
references.note: 2nd edition (Wiley). Emphasises failure modes and multiaxial fatigue; good for the reasoning behind design rules.

references.title: Metal Fatigue in Engineering
references.authors: R. I. Stephens, A. Fatemi, R. R. Stephens and H. O. Fuchs
references.note: 2nd edition (Wiley). The stress-life, strain-life and fracture-mechanics approaches to fatigue in depth.

references.title: Rolling Bearing Analysis
references.authors: T. A. Harris and M. N. Kotzalas
references.note: 5th edition, 2 volumes (CRC Press). The advanced reference on rolling-bearing kinematics, contact stresses, lubrication and life.

references.title: Introduction to the Design and Behavior of Bolted Joints
references.note: 4th edition (CRC Press). Preload, tightening methods, joint stiffness, loosening and fatigue of bolted joints.

references.title: Mechanical Springs
references.note: 2nd edition (McGraw-Hill). The classic treatment of spring stresses, curvature correction, buckling and surge.
